cards.definition: The unit of energy.
A unit of energy equal to 1000 joules.
The type of energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring or foam.
The type of energy stored in a raised object due to its position above the ground.
The type of energy stored in moving objects.
The rate of energy transfer; measured in watts.
The unit of power; 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
A unit of power equal to 1000 watts.
The ability of a substance to store heat energy — the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C.
The proportion of energy supplied that is usefully transferred; efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
The flow of electric charge around a circuit, measured in amps (A).
The unit for electric current.
The amount of work done by a charge when it passes between two points in a circuit.
The measurement of the difficulty for current to flow through a component, measured in ohms (Ω).
The unit of electrical resistance.
A circuit that has branches — current can take more than one path.
The parts of an electric circuit, such as bulbs, resistors and switches.
Electricity where electrons move in one direction only, e.g. from a battery.
Electricity where electrons move forwards and backwards, e.g. from the mains supply.
A circuit with only one path for current to flow — all components are in a single loop.
The equation showing the relationship between voltage, current and resistance: V = IR.
A component that only allows electricity to flow in one direction.
A component that can vary the amount of resistance in a circuit.
A component whose resistance changes with temperature — resistance decreases as temperature increases.
Live (brown), neutral (blue) and earth (green and yellow).
A safety feature in homes that automatically cuts the circuit if too much current flows.
Where electricity is generated by spinning a turbine connected to a generator.
The component that must spin to generate electricity in a power station.
A device that increases voltage and decreases current for efficient transmission across the National Grid.
The voltage supplied to homes in the UK is 230V.
Solid, liquid and gas — the three states in which matter can exist.
Particles that touch but are randomly arranged and can flow — this describes a liquid.
Particles that touch and are arranged in an ordered pattern, vibrating in fixed positions.
Particles that do not touch and are randomly arranged, moving freely at high speed.
The state of matter with the lowest amount of energy.
The state of matter with the lowest density — particles are far apart.
The unit for mass.
The unit for volume.
The unit for density.
Density = mass ÷ volume.
The change of state when a solid turns into a liquid.
The change of state when a liquid turns into a gas.
The change of state when a gas turns into a liquid.
The change of state when a liquid turns into a solid.
Temperature levels off and remains constant during a change of state as energy breaks intermolecular bonds.
The amount of heat energy taken in or given out during a change of state.
When particles gain energy they vibrate more (in solids) or move faster (in liquids and gases).
As temperature increases, particles move faster.
As temperature increases, particles collide more often and with more force, so pressure increases.
The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom — determines which element it is.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
An element with a different mass due to a different number of neutrons.
The breakdown of an unstable isotope, releasing radiation.
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
A helium nucleus consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons; stopped by paper.
A single high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; stopped by aluminium.
A wave of electromagnetic energy from the nucleus; stopped by thick lead.
The equipment used to detect ionising radiation.
An equation showing the changes in atomic number and mass number during radioactive decay.
Gamma radiation is blocked by thick lead.
Alpha radiation is blocked by paper or a few centimetres of air.
Beta radiation is blocked by a few millimetres of aluminium.
The time it takes for the activity of a radioactive substance to decrease by half.
The presence of unwanted radioactive atoms on or inside an object or person.
Exposure to ionising radiation from an external source.
The process used to kill bacteria on food using ionising radiation to extend shelf life.
The unwanted changing of DNA caused by ionising radiation.
A use of irradiation — killing micro-organisms on surgical equipment.
The disease that can be caused by exposure to ionising radiation damaging DNA.
A quantity with magnitude only, e.g. speed, mass, temperature.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, represented by an arrow, e.g. velocity, force.
A force that acts when objects are physically touching, e.g. friction, tension.
A force that acts when objects are physically separated, e.g. gravity, magnetic, electrostatic.
Friction, air and water resistance, and tension are examples of contact forces.
Gravity, electrostatic and magnetic forces are examples of non-contact forces.
The area around an object where gravity acts on other masses.
The single point where the weight of an object is considered to act.
The single force that shows the combined effect of all forces acting on an object.
The force of gravity acting on an object's mass; measured in newtons.
A diagram that shows the scaled resolution of forces acting on an object.
Occurs when a force moves or displaces an object; work done = force × distance.
The relationship between the extension of an elastic object and the force applied is directly proportional.
The point at which Hooke's Law is no longer true — the spring is permanently deformed.
The measurement of distance covered in a given time; speed = distance ÷ time.
The typical speed of sound in air is approximately 330 m/s.
The speed of an object in a given direction — a vector quantity.
The part of a distance-time graph used to calculate speed.
The change in speed (or velocity) of an object over a given time.
Another term for negative acceleration — an object slowing down.
An object with a resultant force of 0N is either stationary or moving at constant speed.
When forces acting on an object are unbalanced, the object accelerates or changes direction.
The forces exerted on two objects that interact are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The distance a vehicle travels while the driver is reacting before applying the brakes.
The distance a vehicle travels after the brakes have been applied until it stops.
The combined distance covered during the thinking time and the braking distance.
Alcohol, drugs and distractions such as phones increase reaction time and thinking distance.
Road conditions, brake condition and tyre condition affect braking distance.
Greater mass and higher speed both increase the braking distance required.
The tendency of an object to keep moving; momentum = mass × velocity.
A wave where the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. light.
A wave where the oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound.
The height of a wave from its undisturbed position to its peak.
The distance between the same position on two adjacent waves.
The number of waves passing a point in one second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Infrared and microwaves are electromagnetic waves used for heating.
Microwaves, radio waves and visible light are used for communication.
X-rays and gamma waves are used for medical purposes such as imaging and treatment.
Radiation that can cause mutations by damaging DNA.
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma waves can all cause cancer by ionising cells.
The ends of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest — north and south.
The result of putting like poles (N-N or S-S) together — they push apart.
The result of putting opposite poles (N-S) together — they pull towards each other.
The area around a magnet where the magnetic force acts on other magnetic materials.
A magnet that is created when a magnetic material is placed in an external magnetic field.
A piece of equipment containing a small magnet that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field to show direction.
A coil of wire with an electric current passing through it — acts like a bar magnet.
A solenoid with an iron core — produces a stronger, controllable magnetic field.
Lines showing the shape and direction of the force around a magnet — always from N to S outside the magnet.
The magnetic field surrounding the Earth that compasses align with; its source is the movement of molten iron in the core.
